title: FAST2: an Intelligent Assistant for Finding Relevant Papers

edges.ref: Yu, Z., Kraft, N. A., and Menzies, T. (2018). Finding better active learners for faster literature reviews. Empirical Software Engineering, pages 1-26.
edges.evidence: four different treatments are tested, including the random sampling tactic from FASTREAD (Yu et al., 2018) as a baseline

edges.target: FASTREAD active learner (Yu et al. 2018) as code base
edges.ref: Yu, Z., Kraft, N. A., and Menzies, T. (2018). Finding better active learners for faster literature reviews. Empirical Software Engineering, pages 1-26.
edges.evidence: we propose our new reading tool FAST2 which is built on top of FASTREAD (Yu et al., 2018)

edges.ref: Yu, Z., Kraft, N. A., and Menzies, T. (2018). Finding better active learners for faster literature reviews. Empirical Software Engineering, pages 1-26.
edges.evidence: FASTREAD reviews up to 50% fewer papers while finding the same number of relevant papers

edges.target: 32 active learners comparison, Figure 2 (Yu et al. 2018)
edges.ref: Yu, Z., Kraft, N. A., and Menzies, T. (2018). Finding better active learners for faster literature reviews. Empirical Software Engineering, pages 1-26.
edges.evidence: Figure 2: Median results (over 30 runs) of 32 active learning algorithms and manual review (linear review) across the four datasets of Table 1.

edges.target: Scott-Knott + nonparametric tests protocol (Yu et al. 2018)
edges.ref: Yu, Z., Kraft, N. A., and Menzies, T. (2018). Finding better active learners for faster literature reviews. Empirical Software Engineering, pages 1-26.
edges.evidence: As suggested in the authors' prior work (Yu et al., 2018), nonparametric hypothesis tests are applied to handle the non-normal distribution.

edges.ref: Cormack, G. V. and Grossman, M. R. (2015). Autonomy and reliability of continuous active learning for technology-assisted review. arXiv preprint arXiv:1504.06868.
edges.evidence: Auto-BM25 is considered as a depreciated version of Rank-BM25 since it never ranks better than Rank-BM25 (worse in three and similarly in one dataset).

edges.ref: Cormack, G. V. and Grossman, M. R. (2015). Autonomy and reliability of continuous active learning for technology-assisted review. arXiv preprint arXiv:1504.06868.
edges.evidence: Auto-Syn is not recommended. It requires human experts to synthesize example relevant text, which is a difficult task.

edges.ref: Cormack, G. V. and Grossman, M. R. (2015). Autonomy and reliability of continuous active learning for technology-assisted review. arXiv preprint arXiv:1504.06868.
edges.evidence: Our solution to this problem is based on presumptive non-relevant examples (shortened as PRESUME in the rest of this paper) proposed in the legal literature by Cormack and Grossman (2015).

edges.ref: Robertson, S., Zaragoza, H., et al. (2009). The probabilistic relevance framework: Bm25 and beyond. Foundations and Trends in Information Retrieval, 3(4):333-389.
edges.evidence: rank the unlabeled examples with their corresponding BM25 scores, which is calculated based on tf-idf (Robertson et al., 2009)

edges.ref: Wallace, B. C., Dahabreh, I. J., Moran, K. H., Brodley, C. E., and Trikalinos, T. A. (2013a). Active literature discovery for scoping evidence reviews: How many needles are there. KDD-DMH.
edges.evidence: The SEMI estimator (in blue) is not only more accurate than the Wallace'13 estimator (in green) but also the estimation from uniform random sampling (in red).

edges.target: Uniform random sampling baseline result (Wallace et al. 2013a)
edges.ref: Wallace, B. C., Dahabreh, I. J., Moran, K. H., Brodley, C. E., and Trikalinos, T. A. (2013a). Active literature discovery for scoping evidence reviews: How many needles are there. KDD-DMH.
edges.evidence: It was observed to estimate more accurately than the Wallace'13 estimator according to Wallace et al. (2013a).

edges.ref: Ros, R., Bjarnason, E., and Runeson, P. (2017). A machine learning approach for semi-automated search and selection in literature studies. EASE 2017, pages 118-127. ACM.
edges.evidence: we observe that Ros'17 usually stops too early and results in a low recall

edges.ref: Cormack, G. V. and Grossman, M. R. (2016a). Engineering quality and reliability in technology-assisted review. SIGIR 2016, pages 75-84. ACM.
edges.evidence: Cormack'16 results in a large range of recalls which the user has no control of

edges.ref: Cormack, G. V. and Grossman, M. R. (2017). Navigating imprecision in relevance assessments on the road to total recall: Roger and me. SIGIR 2017, pages 5-14.
edges.evidence: Cormack'17 is the least stable treatment among the four.

edges.ref: Cormack, G. V. and Grossman, M. R. (2017). Navigating imprecision in relevance assessments on the road to total recall: Roger and me. SIGIR 2017, pages 5-14.
edges.evidence: Cormack and Grossman (2017) concluded that a human reviewer could achieve on the order of 70% recall and 70% precision.

edges.ref: Kuhrmann, M., Fernndez, D. M., and Daneva, M. (2017). On the pragmatic design of literature studies in software engineering: an experience-based guideline. EMSE, 22(6):2852-2891.
edges.evidence: In general, we do not suggest Kuhrmann'17 since recall is most important.

edges.ref: Hall, T., Beecham, S., Bowes, D., Gray, D., and Counsell, S. (2012). A systematic literature review on fault prediction performance in software engineering. IEEE TSE, 38(6):1276-1304.
edges.evidence: Previously, we have created three datasets by reverse-engineering existing SLRs (Yu et al., 2018) ... Hall dataset from Hall et al. (2012)

edges.ref: Wahono, R. S. (2015). A systematic literature review of software defect prediction: research trends, datasets, methods and frameworks. Journal of Software Engineering, 1(1):1-16.
edges.evidence: Wahono dataset from Wahono (2015) ... In this paper, we use the same four datasets to evaluate different techniques.

edges.ref: Radjenović, D., Heričko, M., Torkar, R., and Živkovič, A. (2013). Software fault prediction metrics: A systematic literature review. IST, 55(8):1397-1418.
edges.evidence: Radjenović dataset from Radjenović et al. (2013). Apart from the three created datasets, one dataset (Kitchenham) is provided directly

edges.ref: Kitchenham, B. and Brereton, P. (2013). A systematic review of systematic review process research in software engineering. IST, 55(12):2049-2075.
edges.evidence: one dataset (Kitchenham) is provided directly by the author of Kitchenham and Brereton (2013)
the LogisticRegression function is implemented with scikit-learn, and its regularization strength C is calculated as C = |RE|/(|L|-|LR|)

edges.ref: Yu, Z. and Menzies, T. (2017). fastread/src: Fast2. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.1184123.
edges.evidence: All the above datasets are available online (Yu and Menzies, 2017).

edges.ref: Scott, A. J. and Knott, M. (1974). A cluster analysis method for grouping means in the analysis of variance. Biometrics, pages 507-512.
edges.evidence: Scott-Knott analysis was applied to cluster and rank the performance (X95) of each treatment.

edges.ref: Mittas, N. and Angelis, L. (2013). Ranking and clustering software cost estimation models through a multiple comparisons algorithm. IEEE TSE, 39(4):537-551.
edges.evidence: As recommended by Mittas & Angelis in their 2013 IEEE TSE paper (Mittas and Angelis, 2013), Scott-Knott analysis was applied

edges.ref: Efron, B. (1982). The jackknife, the bootstrap and other resampling plans. SIAM.
edges.evidence: Scott-Knott decided two methods are not of little difference if both bootstrapping (Efron, 1982), and an effect size test (Cliff, 1993) agreed

edges.ref: Cliff, N. (1993). Dominance statistics: Ordinal analyses to answer ordinal questions. Psychological Bulletin, 114(3):494.
edges.evidence: not a negligible effect (Cliff's Delta >= 0.147)

edges.ref: Cohen, A. M. (2011). Performance of support-vector-machine-based classification on 15 systematic review topics evaluated with the wss@95 measure. JAMIA, 18(1):104-104.
edges.evidence: our success criteria is "work saved oversampling at 95% recall" (WSS@95) (Cohen, 2011)

edges.ref: Kitchenham, B. (2004). Procedures for performing systematic reviews. Keele, UK, Keele University, 33(2004):1-26.
edges.evidence: in the terminology of Kitchenham's systematic literature review (SLR) (Kitchenham, 2004) framework, this "initial skim" is the primary study selection phase

edges.ref: Feldt, R. and Magazinius, A. (2010). Validity threats in empirical software engineering research-an initial survey. In SEKE, pages 374-379.
edges.evidence: There are several validity threats to the design of this study (Feldt and Magazinius, 2010).

edges.target: One minute per paper estimate (Shemilt et al. 2016)
edges.ref: Shemilt, I., Khan, N., Park, S., and Thomas, J. (2016). Use of cost-effectiveness analysis to compare the efficiency of study identification methods in systematic reviews. Systematic reviews, 5(1):140.
edges.evidence: Shemilt et al. (2016) estimated that assessing one paper for relevancy takes at least one minute.

edges.ref: Wohlin, C. (2014). Guidelines for snowballing in systematic literature studies and a replication in software engineering. EASE 2014, page 38. ACM.
edges.evidence: Wohlin reported in one of his studies as precision to be 6.8% (Wohlin, 2014) while in another study as precision to be 15/64 = 23.4%

edges.target: Semi-supervised recall <95% at 30% labeled (Liu et al. 2016)
edges.ref: Liu, J., Timsina, P., and El-Gayar, O. (2016). A comparative analysis of semi-supervised learning: The case of article selection for medical systematic reviews. Information Systems Frontiers.
edges.evidence: Liu et al. (2016) reported a less than 95% recall with 30% data labeled

edges.target: Select-papers is hardest SLR step (Carver et al. 2013)
edges.ref: Carver, J. C., Hassler, E., Hernandes, E., and Kraft, N. A. (2013). Identifying barriers to the systematic literature review process. ESEM 2013, pages 203-212. IEEE.
edges.evidence: Carver et al. (2013) polled researchers who have conducted literature reviews. According to their votes, select papers was one of the hardest, most time-consuming tasks

edges.target: Abstract-based methods outperform alternatives (Kanoulas et al. 2017; Roegiest et al. 2015)
edges.ref: Kanoulas, E., Li, D., Azzopardi, L., and Spijker, R. (2017). Overview of the CLEF technologically assisted reviews in empirical medicine. CLEF 2017 Working Notes.
edges.evidence: Several studies show that the performance of abstract-based methods is better than other approaches (Kanoulas et al., 2017; Roegiest et al., 2015).

edges.target: Class probability estimates unreliable for imbalanced data (Wallace & Dahabreh 2012)
edges.ref: Wallace, B. C. and Dahabreh, I. J. (2012). Class probability estimates are unreliable for imbalanced data (and how to fix them). ICDM 2012, pages 695-704. IEEE.
edges.evidence: The challenges for building such a class probability estimator include the class imbalance of training data (Wallace and Dahabreh, 2012)

edges.target: 95% recall accepted in evidence-based medicine (O'Mara-Eves et al. 2015)
edges.ref: O'Mara-Eves, A., Thomas, J., McNaught, J., Miwa, M., and Ananiadou, S. (2015). Using text mining for study identification in systematic reviews. Systematic reviews, 4(1):5.
edges.evidence: 0.95 recall is usually considered acceptable in evidence-based medicine (Cohen, 2011; Cohen et al., 2006; O'Mara-Eves et al., 2015)

not_reuse_examples: Di Nunzio (2018) stopping strategy: explicitly NOT compared ('requires the review to follow the order of BM25, therefore is not compared').
Wallace 2010b / Miwa 2014 / Cormack & Grossman 2014: the active learners FASTREAD was built from; in this paper only cited as background, the paper runs FASTREAD not them.
Marshall et al. (2015), Abstrackr/EPPI-Reviewer/Rayyan tool citations, Chapelle (2017), Voorhees (2000): background/definition only, nothing executed or adopted.
notes: Tool paper extending the authors' own FASTREAD (Yu et al. 2018) with three add-ons; nearly all baselines (Cormack&Grossman seeding/knee/error-correction, Wallace'13, Ros'17, Kuhrmann'17) are re-implemented and shown worse (refutes); datasets are the same four SLR sets from the prior self work.
